True Statement: Health does not simply mean 'absence of disease' or 'physical fitness'; it is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being.
False 1: Health simply means 'absence of disease' or 'physical fitness'.
False 2: Health is a state of complete physical and mental well-being, not social well-being.

True Statement: When people are healthy, they are more efficient at work, which increases productivity and brings economic prosperity.
False 1: When people are healthy, they are less efficient at work, which decreases productivity.
False 2: Health increases productivity but does not affect economic prosperity.

True Statement: Health also increases longevity of people and reduces infant and maternal mortality.
False 1: Health decreases longevity of people and increases infant and maternal mortality.
False 2: Health increases longevity but does not affect infant or maternal mortality.

True Statement: Balanced diet, personal hygiene and regular exercise are very important to maintain good health.
False 1: Only regular exercise, not balanced diet or personal hygiene, is important to maintain good health.
False 2: Balanced diet alone, without personal hygiene or exercise, is sufficient to maintain good health.

True Statement: Diseases can be broadly grouped into infectious and non-infectious.
False 1: Diseases can only be grouped as bacterial and viral diseases.
False 2: Diseases cannot be categorised as infectious or non-infectious — all diseases are transmitted.

True Statement: Diseases which are easily transmitted from one person to another are called infectious diseases.
False 1: Diseases which are not transmitted from one person to another are called infectious diseases.
False 2: Non-infectious diseases are easily transmitted from one person to another.

True Statement: Among non-infectious diseases, cancer is the major cause of death.
False 1: Among non-infectious diseases, drug abuse is the major cause of death.
False 2: Cancer is a major infectious disease and the leading cause of death.

True Statement: Disease-causing organisms are called pathogens.
False 1: Disease-causing organisms are called commensals.
False 2: Disease-causing organisms are called vectors.

True Statement: Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium which causes typhoid fever in human beings.
False 1: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a pathogenic bacterium which causes typhoid fever in human beings.
False 2: Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium which causes pneumonia in human beings.

True Statement: Salmonella typhi pathogens generally enter the small intestine through food and water contaminated with them and migrate to other organs through blood.
False 1: Salmonella typhi pathogens generally enter the large intestine through contaminated food and water.
False 2: Salmonella typhi pathogens generally enter the respiratory tract through contaminated food and water.

True Statement: Symptoms of typhoid include sustained high fever (39°C to 40°C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite.
False 1: Symptoms of typhoid include sustained high fever (39°C to 40°C), weakness, stomach pain, diarrhoea, headache and loss of appetite.
False 2: Typhoid is characterised by mild low-grade fever (around 37°C) and mild discomfort.

True Statement: Typhoid fever could be confirmed by Widal test.
False 1: Typhoid fever could be confirmed by ELISA test.
False 2: Pneumonia could be confirmed by Widal test.

True Statement: Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary) was a cook by profession who was a typhoid carrier and spread typhoid for several years through the food she prepared.
False 1: Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary) was a nurse by profession who was a typhoid carrier.
False 2: Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary) was a typhoid patient who fell ill herself, not a carrier.

True Statement: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are responsible for pneumonia in humans, which infects the alveoli of the lungs.
False 1: Salmonella typhi and Haemophilus influenzae are responsible for pneumonia in humans.
False 2: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are responsible for typhoid in humans.
False 3: Streptococcus pneumoniae infects the bronchi (not the alveoli) of the lungs.

True Statement: As a result of pneumonia infection, the alveoli get filled with fluid leading to severe problems in respiration.
False 1: As a result of pneumonia infection, the alveoli get filled with air leading to severe problems in respiration.
False 2: As a result of pneumonia infection, the alveoli get filled with fluid leading to severe problems in digestion.

True Statement: Symptoms of pneumonia include fever, chills, cough and headache; in severe cases the lips and finger nails may turn gray to bluish in colour.
False 1: Symptoms of pneumonia include constipation, abdominal pain and loss of appetite.
False 2: In severe cases of pneumonia, the lips and finger nails may turn red to pink in colour.

True Statement: A healthy person acquires pneumonia by inhaling droplets/aerosols released by an infected person or by sharing glasses and utensils with an infected person.
False 1: A healthy person acquires pneumonia through the bite of an insect vector.
False 2: A healthy person acquires pneumonia only through contaminated food and water.

True Statement: Rhino viruses cause one of the most infectious human ailments — the common cold — and infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs.
False 1: Rhino viruses cause pneumonia in humans and infect the alveoli of the lungs.
False 2: Rhino viruses infect the nose, respiratory passage and the lungs.
False 3: Streptococcus pneumoniae causes one of the most infectious ailments — the common cold.

True Statement: Common cold symptoms include nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache and tiredness, usually lasting for 3–7 days.
False 1: Common cold symptoms usually last for 1–2 days.
False 2: Common cold symptoms usually last for 10–14 days.

True Statement: Common cold is transmitted through contaminated objects such as pens, books, cups, doorknobs, computer keyboard or mouse.
False 1: Common cold can only be transmitted by direct inhalation of droplets from an infected person, not through contaminated objects.
False 2: Common cold is transmitted only through contaminated food and water, not through contaminated objects.

True Statement: Plasmodium, a tiny protozoan, is responsible for malaria.
False 1: Entamoeba histolytica, a tiny protozoan, is responsible for malaria.
False 2: Wuchereria, a filarial worm, is responsible for malaria.

True Statement: Different species of Plasmodium — P. vivax, P. malariae and P. falciparum — are responsible for different types of malaria.
False 1: Only one species of Plasmodium — P. falciparum — is responsible for all types of malaria.
False 2: Different species of Plasmodium — P. vivax, P. malariae and P. bancrofti — are responsible for different types of malaria.

True Statement: Malignant malaria is caused by Plasmodium falciparum and is the most serious form.
False 1: Malignant malaria is caused by Plasmodium vivax and is the most serious form.
False 2: Malignant malaria is caused by Plasmodium malariae and is the most serious form.

True Statement: Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites (infectious form) through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquito.
False 1: Plasmodium enters the human body as merozoites through the bite of the infected female Anopheles mosquito.
False 2: Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites through the bite of infected male Anopheles mosquito.
False 3: Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites through the bite of infected female Aedes mosquito.

True Statement: The parasites initially multiply within the liver cells and then attack the red blood cells (RBCs) resulting in their rupture.
False 1: The parasites initially multiply within the red blood cells and then attack the liver cells.
False 2: The parasites initially multiply within the liver cells and then attack the white blood cells (WBCs).

True Statement: The rupture of RBCs is associated with release of a toxic substance haemozoin, which is responsible for chill and high fever recurring every three to four days.
False 1: The rupture of RBCs is associated with release of haemoglobin, which is responsible for chill and high fever.
False 2: Haemozoin released on rupture of RBCs causes fever recurring every one to two days.

True Statement: The parasites multiply within mosquitoes to form sporozoites that are stored in their salivary glands.
False 1: The parasites multiply within mosquitoes to form merozoites stored in their salivary glands.
False 2: The parasites multiply within mosquitoes to form sporozoites stored in their midgut.

True Statement: The malarial parasite requires two hosts — human and mosquitoes — to complete its life cycle.
False 1: The malarial parasite requires three hosts to complete its life cycle.
False 2: The malarial parasite requires only one host — the human — to complete its life cycle.
False 3: The malarial parasite requires two hosts — human and houseflies — to complete its life cycle.

True Statement: The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector (transmitting agent) for malaria.
False 1: The female Aedes mosquito is the vector for malaria.
False 2: The male Anopheles mosquito is the vector for malaria.

True Statement: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite in the large intestine of humans which causes amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery).
False 1: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite in the small intestine of humans which causes amoebiasis.
False 2: Plasmodium is a protozoan parasite in the large intestine of humans which causes amoebiasis.
False 3: Entamoeba histolytica causes malaria, not amoebiasis.

True Statement: Symptoms of amoebiasis include constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucous and blood clots.
False 1: Symptoms of amoebiasis include sustained high fever, headache and loss of appetite.
False 2: Symptoms of amoebiasis include loose stools with no mucous or blood.

True Statement: Houseflies act as mechanical carriers and transmit the amoebiasis parasite from faeces of infected persons to food and food products.
False 1: Mosquitoes act as mechanical carriers and transmit the amoebiasis parasite from faeces to food products.
False 2: Houseflies act as biological vectors (not mechanical carriers) for transmitting amoebiasis.

True Statement: Ascaris, the common round worm, is an intestinal parasite that causes ascariasis.
False 1: Wuchereria, the filarial worm, is an intestinal parasite that causes ascariasis.
False 2: Ascaris causes filariasis, not ascariasis.

True Statement: Symptoms of ascariasis include internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anemia and blockage of the intestinal passage.
False 1: Symptoms of ascariasis include chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels and gross deformities of lower limbs.
False 2: Symptoms of ascariasis include constipation, abdominal pain and blood in stools.

True Statement: Eggs of Ascaris are excreted along with the faeces of infected persons which contaminate soil, water, plants, etc.
False 1: Larvae (not eggs) of Ascaris are excreted along with the faeces of infected persons.
False 2: Eggs of Wuchereria are excreted along with the faeces of infected persons.

True Statement: Wuchereria (W. bancrofti and W. malayi), the filarial worms, cause a slowly developing chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs — called elephantiasis or filariasis.
False 1: Ascaris causes a slowly developing chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs.
False 2: Wuchereria causes rapidly developing acute inflammation of the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs.
False 3: Wuchereria causes slowly developing chronic inflammation of the blood vessels of the lower limbs.

True Statement: Filarial worms are transmitted to a healthy person through the bite of female mosquito vectors.
False 1: Filarial worms are transmitted through houseflies.
False 2: Filarial worms are transmitted through contaminated food and water.

True Statement: Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton are responsible for ringworms.
False 1: Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton are responsible for filariasis.
False 2: Entamoeba histolytica, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton are responsible for ringworms.

True Statement: Ringworms appear as dry, scaly lesions on skin, nails and scalp accompanied by intense itching.
False 1: Ringworms appear as moist, fluid-filled blisters on skin, nails and scalp.
False 2: Ringworms appear as dry, scaly lesions accompanied by mild burning sensation, not itching.

True Statement: Heat and moisture help fungi to grow, making them thrive in skin folds such as groin or between the toes.
False 1: Cold and dry conditions help fungi to grow, making them thrive in skin folds.
False 2: Heat and moisture help bacteria to grow, making them thrive in skin folds such as groin or between the toes.

True Statement: Ringworms are generally acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or comb of infected individuals.
False 1: Ringworms are generally acquired through the bite of infected mosquitoes.
False 2: Ringworms cannot be acquired from soil or objects used by infected individuals.

True Statement: For diseases like malaria and filariasis transmitted through insect vectors, the most important measure is to control or eliminate vectors and their breeding places.
False 1: For diseases like malaria and filariasis, treatment with antibiotics is the most important measure.
False 2: For diseases like typhoid and amoebiasis, the most important measure is vector control.

True Statement: Gambusia fish introduced in ponds feed on mosquito larvae.
False 1: Rohu fish introduced in ponds feed on mosquito larvae.
False 2: Gambusia fish introduced in ponds are used to chemically disinfect water.

True Statement: The use of vaccines and immunisation programmes have enabled us to completely eradicate smallpox.
False 1: The use of vaccines have enabled us to completely eradicate polio.
False 2: Vaccination programmes have only partially controlled smallpox but could not eradicate it.

True Statement: The overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system, is called immunity.
False 1: The overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms is called allergy.
False 2: The overall inability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms is called immunity.

True Statement: Immunity is of two types: innate immunity and acquired immunity.
False 1: Immunity is of only one type: innate immunity.
False 2: Immunity is of two types: active immunity and passive immunity.

True Statement: Innate immunity is a non-specific type of defence that is present at the time of birth.
False 1: Innate immunity is pathogen-specific type of defence present at the time of birth.
False 2: Acquired immunity is a non-specific type of defence present at the time of birth.

True Statement: Innate immunity consists of four types of barriers: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers.
False 1: Innate immunity consists of three types of barriers: physical, physiological and cellular.
False 2: Innate immunity consists of four types: physical, chemical, cellular and cytokine barriers.

True Statement: Skin on our body is the main physical barrier which prevents entry of micro-organisms.
False 1: Mucus coating of the epithelium is the main physical barrier which prevents entry of micro-organisms.
False 2: Skin on our body is the main physiological barrier which prevents entry of micro-organisms.

True Statement: Mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts helps in trapping microbes entering our body.
False 1: Mucus coating of the epithelium helps in killing microbes, not trapping them.
False 2: Mucus coating of the epithelium lining only the respiratory tract helps in trapping microbes.

True Statement: Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth, tears from eyes — all prevent microbial growth (physiological barriers).
False 1: Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth, tears from eyes — all promote microbial growth.
False 2: Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth and tears from eyes are cellular barriers, not physiological barriers.

True Statement: Polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils), monocytes and natural killer cells can phagocytose and destroy microbes (cellular barriers).
False 1: Polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes and natural killer cells are cytokine barriers.
False 2: PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes and natural killer cells secrete interferons to protect against viral infection.

True Statement: Virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection (cytokine barriers).
False 1: Virus-infected cells secrete interferons which help viral infection spread to non-infected cells.
False 2: Macrophages secrete proteins called interferons which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.

True Statement: Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific and characterised by memory.
False 1: Acquired immunity is non-specific and not characterised by memory.
False 2: Innate immunity is pathogen-specific and characterised by memory.

True Statement: When the body encounters a pathogen for the first time, it produces a primary response which is of low intensity.
False 1: When the body encounters a pathogen for the first time, it produces a primary response which is of high intensity.
False 2: When the body encounters a pathogen for the first time, it produces a secondary (anamnestic) response.

True Statement: Subsequent encounter with the same pathogen elicits a highly intensified secondary or anamnestic response.
False 1: Subsequent encounter with the same pathogen elicits a low-intensity secondary response.
False 2: Subsequent encounter with the same pathogen elicits the same low-intensity primary response.

True Statement: B-lymphocytes produce proteins called antibodies in response to pathogens into the blood.
False 1: T-lymphocytes produce proteins called antibodies in response to pathogens.
False 2: B-lymphocytes produce proteins called interferons in response to pathogens.

True Statement: T-cells themselves do not secrete antibodies but help B cells to produce them.
False 1: T-cells secrete antibodies directly and also help B cells to produce them.
False 2: B-cells do not secrete antibodies but help T-cells to produce them.

True Statement: Each antibody molecule has four peptide chains — two small called light chains and two longer called heavy chains.
False 1: Each antibody molecule has four peptide chains — two longer called light chains and two small called heavy chains.
False 2: Each antibody molecule has two peptide chains — one light chain and one heavy chain.

True Statement: An antibody is represented as H₂L₂.
False 1: An antibody is represented as H₂L₃.
False 2: An antibody is represented as H₄L₄.

True Statement: IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG are some of the types of antibodies produced in our body.
False 1: IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG are some of the types of interferons produced in our body.
False 2: IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG are types of allergens, not antibodies.

True Statement: Because antibodies are found in the blood, the response is called humoral immune response.
False 1: Because antibodies are found in the blood, the response is called cell-mediated immune response.
False 2: Antibodies are found in the lymph nodes, which is why the response is called humoral immune response.

True Statement: T-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity (CMI).
False 1: B-lymphocytes mediate cell-mediated immunity (CMI).
False 2: T-lymphocytes mediate humoral immune response.

True Statement: Cell-mediated immune response is responsible for graft rejection.
False 1: Humoral immune response is responsible for graft rejection.
False 2: Cell-mediated immune response promotes graft acceptance.

True Statement: Active immunity is produced when a host is exposed to antigens; it is slow and takes time to give full effective response.
False 1: Passive immunity is produced when a host is exposed to antigens; it is slow and takes time.
False 2: Active immunity is rapid and gives immediate full effective response upon first exposure.

True Statement: When ready-made antibodies are directly given to protect the body against foreign agents, it is called passive immunity.
False 1: When ready-made antibodies are directly given to protect the body, it is called active immunity.
False 2: When a host produces its own antibodies after antigen exposure, it is called passive immunity.

True Statement: The yellowish fluid colostrum secreted by mother during the initial days of lactation has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant.
False 1: Colostrum has abundant antibodies of IgG type to protect the infant.
False 2: Colostrum has abundant interferons (not antibodies) to protect the infant.

True Statement: The foetus also receives some antibodies from the mother through the placenta during pregnancy.
False 1: The foetus receives antibodies from the mother through the umbilical cord during pregnancy.
False 2: The foetus does not receive any antibodies from the mother during pregnancy.

True Statement: In vaccination, a preparation of antigenic proteins of pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen is introduced into the body.
False 1: In vaccination, a live and fully active pathogen is introduced into the body.
False 2: In vaccination, ready-made antibodies are introduced into the body.

True Statement: Vaccines generate memory B and T-cells that recognise the pathogen quickly on subsequent exposure and overwhelm the invaders with a massive production of antibodies.
False 1: Vaccines do not generate memory cells; they only provide immediate short-term protection.
False 2: Vaccines generate memory NK cells that recognise the pathogen quickly on subsequent exposure.

True Statement: For quick immune response to tetanus, preformed antibodies or antitoxin (containing antibodies to the toxin) are directly injected — this is passive immunisation.
False 1: For quick immune response to tetanus, a vaccine with weakened pathogen is injected — this is passive immunisation.
False 2: Injecting preformed antibodies directly into a patient is called active immunisation.

True Statement: In cases of snakebites, the injection given to patients contains preformed antibodies against snake venom.
False 1: In cases of snakebites, the injection given to patients contains an inactivated form of the snake venom as a vaccine.
False 2: In cases of snakebites, the injection given to patients contains anti-histamines to prevent allergic reaction.

True Statement: Hepatitis B vaccine is produced from yeast using recombinant DNA technology.
False 1: Hepatitis B vaccine is produced from bacteria using recombinant DNA technology.
False 2: Polio vaccine is produced from yeast using recombinant DNA technology.

True Statement: The exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens in the environment is called allergy.
False 1: The normal response of the immune system to certain antigens in the environment is called allergy.
False 2: The exaggerated response of the immune system to self-cells is called allergy.

True Statement: The substances to which the exaggerated immune response is produced are called allergens.
False 1: The substances to which the exaggerated immune response is produced are called antigens.
False 2: Allergens are the antibodies produced against environmental antigens.

True Statement: The antibodies produced against allergens are of IgE type.
False 1: The antibodies produced against allergens are of IgG type.
False 2: The antibodies produced against allergens are of IgA type.

True Statement: Allergy is due to the release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from the mast cells.
False 1: Allergy is due to the release of chemicals like interferons and antibodies from the mast cells.
False 2: Allergy is due to the release of histamine and serotonin from lymphocytes.
False 3: Allergy is due to the decreased release of histamine and serotonin from the mast cells.

True Statement: Drugs like anti-histamine, adrenalin and steroids quickly reduce the symptoms of allergy.
False 1: Drugs like antibiotics and interferons quickly reduce the symptoms of allergy.
False 2: Drugs like anti-histamine, adrenalin and steroids quickly reduce the symptoms of cancer.

True Statement: Sometimes the body attacks self-cells due to genetic and other unknown reasons, resulting in damage called auto-immune disease.
False 1: Sometimes the body attacks self-cells, resulting in enhanced immunity and better protection against pathogens.
False 2: The body attacking foreign organisms is called auto-immune disease.

True Statement: Rheumatoid arthritis is an auto-immune disease.
False 1: Rheumatoid arthritis is an infectious disease.
False 2: Cancer is an auto-immune disease.

True Statement: Primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes.
False 1: Primary lymphoid organs are spleen and lymph nodes where immature lymphocytes differentiate.
False 2: Secondary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus where immature lymphocytes differentiate.
False 3: Primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus where mature lymphocytes proliferate into effector cells.

True Statement: Secondary lymphoid organs include spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of small intestine and appendix.
False 1: Primary lymphoid organs include spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches and appendix.
False 2: Secondary lymphoid organs include spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of large intestine and appendix.

True Statement: The thymus is a lobed organ located near the heart and beneath the breastbone.
False 1: The thymus is a lobed organ located near the kidneys and beneath the breastbone.
False 2: The spleen is a lobed organ located near the heart and beneath the breastbone.

True Statement: The thymus is quite large at birth but keeps reducing in size with age and reduces to a very small size by puberty.
False 1: The thymus is quite small at birth but keeps increasing in size with age.
False 2: The thymus remains constant in size throughout life.

True Statement: The spleen is a large bean-shaped organ that mainly contains lymphocytes and phagocytes and acts as a filter of the blood.
False 1: The thymus is a large bean-shaped organ that mainly contains lymphocytes and phagocytes.
False 2: The spleen acts as a filter of the lymph, not the blood.

True Statement: The spleen also has a large reservoir of erythrocytes.
False 1: The spleen also has a large reservoir of lymphocytes.
False 2: The thymus also has a large reservoir of erythrocytes.

True Statement: Lymph nodes serve to trap micro-organisms or other antigens which happen to get into the lymph and tissue fluid.
False 1: Lymph nodes serve to produce B and T lymphocytes directly from stem cells.
False 2: The spleen serves to trap micro-organisms that get into the lymph and tissue fluid.

True Statement: MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) is located within the lining of major tracts and constitutes about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in human body.
False 1: MALT constitutes about 70 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in human body.
False 2: MALT constitutes about 25 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in human body.

True Statement: AIDS stands for Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome.
False 1: AIDS stands for Acquired Immuno Deficiency Symptoms.
False 2: AIDS stands for Acquired Immuno-sufficiency Syndrome.

True Statement: AIDS is not a congenital disease; it is acquired during the lifetime of an individual.
False 1: AIDS is a congenital disease inherited from parents at birth.
False 2: AIDS is classified as a congenital disease because it is caused by a virus.

True Statement: AIDS was first reported in 1981.
False 1: AIDS was first reported in 1971.
False 2: AIDS was first reported in 1991.

True Statement: AIDS has spread all over the world killing more than 25 million persons.
False 1: AIDS has spread all over the world killing more than 50 million persons.
False 2: AIDS has spread only in certain regions of the world, killing about 5 million persons.

True Statement: AIDS is caused by HIV (Human Immuno deficiency Virus), a member of a group of viruses called retrovirus, which have an envelope enclosing the RNA genome.
False 1: AIDS is caused by HIV, a member of the herpes virus group.
False 2: AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus which has DNA genome.
False 3: AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus with no envelope, enclosing an RNA genome.

True Statement: Transmission of HIV occurs by sexual contact with infected person, transfusion of contaminated blood, sharing infected needles, and from infected mother to child through placenta.
False 1: HIV/AIDS spreads by mere touch or physical contact with an infected person.
False 2: HIV is transmitted only through sexual contact; blood transfusion and sharing needles are not routes.

True Statement: HIV/AIDS is not spread by mere touch or physical contact; it spreads only through body fluids.
False 1: HIV/AIDS spreads by mere touch or physical contact with an infected person.
False 2: HIV/AIDS spreads through air, just like the common cold.

True Statement: The time-lag between HIV infection and appearance of AIDS symptoms may vary from a few months to many years, usually 5–10 years.
False 1: The time-lag between HIV infection and AIDS symptoms is usually 1–2 years.
False 2: The time-lag between HIV infection and AIDS symptoms is usually 15–20 years.

True Statement: After entering the body, HIV enters macrophages where RNA genome of the virus replicates to form viral DNA with the help of the enzyme reverse transcriptase.
False 1: After entering the body, HIV enters T-lymphocytes (not macrophages) where RNA replicates to form viral DNA.
False 2: After entering the body, HIV RNA replicates to form viral DNA with the help of DNA polymerase.

True Statement: Viral DNA gets incorporated into host cell's DNA and directs infected cells to produce virus particles.
False 1: Viral RNA (not DNA) gets incorporated directly into the host cell's DNA.
False 2: Viral DNA remains separate in the cytoplasm and does not incorporate into host cell's DNA.

True Statement: HIV also enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses that attack other helper T-lymphocytes, leading to a progressive decrease in their number.
False 1: HIV also enters B-lymphocytes, replicates and produces progeny viruses that attack other B-lymphocytes.
False 2: HIV leads to a progressive increase in the number of helper T-lymphocytes.

True Statement: Due to decrease in helper T-lymphocytes, the person suffers from infections due to bacteria especially Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and parasites like Toxoplasma.
False 1: Due to decrease in helper T-lymphocytes, the person develops stronger immunity against all infections.
False 2: Due to decrease in B-lymphocytes, the person suffers from infections due to Mycobacterium and Toxoplasma.

True Statement: A widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is ELISA (enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay).
False 1: A widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is the Widal test.
False 2: ELISA is a widely used diagnostic test for typhoid fever.

True Statement: Treatment of AIDS with anti-retroviral drugs is only partially effective; they can only prolong the life of the patient but cannot prevent death.
False 1: Anti-retroviral drugs are fully effective and can completely cure AIDS.
False 2: Anti-retroviral drugs can prevent death in AIDS patients by fully eliminating the virus.

True Statement: Normal cells show a property called contact inhibition by virtue of which contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth.
False 1: Cancer cells show a property called contact inhibition that inhibits their uncontrolled growth.
False 2: Normal cells show a property called contact promotion which promotes their controlled growth.

True Statement: Cancer cells appear to have lost the property of contact inhibition.
False 1: Cancer cells retain the property of contact inhibition.
False 2: Normal cells have lost the property of contact inhibition.

True Statement: Benign tumors remain confined to their original location and do not spread to other parts of the body.
False 1: Malignant tumors remain confined to their original location and do not spread to other parts.
False 2: Benign tumors spread to other parts of the body and cause major damage.

True Statement: The malignant tumors are a mass of proliferating cells called neoplastic or tumor cells that grow very rapidly, invading and damaging surrounding normal tissues.
False 1: Benign tumors are a mass of proliferating neoplastic cells that grow very rapidly and invade surrounding tissues.
False 2: Malignant tumor cells grow very slowly and do not invade surrounding normal tissues.

True Statement: Cells sloughed from malignant tumors reach distant sites through blood and start new tumors there — this property is called metastasis.
False 1: Cells sloughed from benign tumors reach distant sites through blood and start new tumors — called metastasis.
False 2: Cells from malignant tumors do not spread through blood; they remain confined to the original location.
False 3: Cells sloughed from malignant tumors reach distant sites through lymph (not blood) and start new tumors.

True Statement: Metastasis is the most feared property of malignant tumors.
False 1: Loss of contact inhibition is the most feared property of malignant tumors.
False 2: Metastasis is the most feared property of benign tumors.

True Statement: Physical carcinogens include ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays and non-ionising radiations like UV.
False 1: UV radiation is a type of ionising radiation that causes DNA damage leading to cancer.
False 2: Tobacco smoke and chemicals are physical carcinogens.

True Statement: Chemical carcinogens present in tobacco smoke have been identified as a major cause of lung cancer.
False 1: Chemical carcinogens in tobacco smoke are a major cause of breast cancer.
False 2: Tobacco smoke does not contain any carcinogens and is not linked to lung cancer.

True Statement: Cancer-causing viruses called oncogenic viruses have genes called viral oncogenes.
False 1: Oncogenic viruses have genes called cellular oncogenes (not viral oncogenes).
False 2: Oncogenic viruses prevent cancer by suppressing cellular oncogenes.

True Statement: Cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto oncogenes are found in normal cells and when activated can lead to oncogenic transformation.
False 1: Proto oncogenes are found only in cancer cells and not in normal cells.
False 2: Proto oncogenes prevent cancer when activated; they cause cancer only when suppressed.

True Statement: CT (computed tomography) uses X-rays to generate a three-dimensional image of the internals of an object.
False 1: CT uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to generate a three-dimensional image.
False 2: MRI uses X-rays to generate a three-dimensional image of the internals of an object.

True Statement: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue.
False 1: MRI uses X-rays and ionising radiations to detect pathological changes in living tissue.
False 2: CT uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to detect pathological changes in living tissue.

True Statement: In radiotherapy, tumor cells are irradiated lethally while taking proper care of the normal tissues surrounding the tumor.
False 1: In radiotherapy, both tumor cells and surrounding normal tissues are irradiated lethally.
False 2: In radiotherapy, tumor cells are treated with chemicals instead of radiation.
